title: Pod Networking Model
summary: Every Pod gets its own IP, Pods talk without NAT, CNI plugins build the Pod network and kube-proxy programs Service traffic.

items: Every Pod gets its **own IP address**, unique across the whole cluster.
All containers in a Pod share **one network namespace**, so they reach each other over `localhost`.
Any Pod can reach any other Pod, on the same node or a different one, **directly: no proxies and no NAT** (unless the network is deliberately segmented).
Node agents such as the kubelet and system daemons can reach every Pod on their own node.
Pods behave much like VMs or hosts: no need to link containers or map container ports to host ports.

blocks.text: The **Service** API adds a stable IP or hostname in front of Pods that come and go. **EndpointSlices** track which Pods currently back a Service. **NetworkPolicy** controls traffic between Pods.
Giving each Pod its own IP avoids the pain of coordinating host ports between many apps sharing the same machines.
Kubernetes defines the APIs, but most of the networking is done by external components.

rows: A Pod network implementation, usually a **CNI plugin**
**kube-proxy** by default, or the network plugin's own proxy
Gateway API or Ingress implementations, or `type: LoadBalancer` on a supported cloud

blocks.text: If your network plugin doesn't support NetworkPolicy, you can still create NetworkPolicy objects, but they **have no effect**.
Pods, Services and Nodes need **non-overlapping** IP ranges, each handed out by a different component:

items: Clusters are IPv4 only, IPv6 only, or dual-stack (IPv4/IPv6 or IPv6/IPv4).
In dual-stack, all three components assign both families and must agree on the **primary** IP family.
Kubernetes only counts the IPs listed in `node.status.addresses` and `pod.status.ips`, even if an interface has more.
A **CNI plugin is required** to implement the network model. Pick one compatible with your cluster.
It must support CNI spec **v0.4.0 or later**; v1.0.0 compatibility is recommended.
The **container runtime** (for example containerd or CRI-O) is configured to load the CNI plugins, not the kubelet.
The kubelet flags `cni-bin-dir` and `network-plugin` were **removed in v1.24**.
Runtimes must also give every sandbox a loopback interface `lo` (the CNI loopback plugin can do this).
`hostPort` support comes from the `portmap` plugin with the `portMappings` capability.

blocks.text: Pods stuck without networking on a node? Check that a CNI config exists in `/etc/cni/net.d` and the binaries in `/opt/cni/bin`. Since v1.24 the runtime, not the kubelet, loads CNI.

**kube-proxy** runs on every node (unless replaced by another component). It watches **Service and EndpointSlice** objects and programs node rules that catch traffic sent to a Service's `clusterIP` and port and send it on to a backend. It handles every Service type **except ExternalName**.

rows: Default in v1.37 when no mode is set. Picks a backend at random by default.
Successor to iptables; needs kernel 5.13+. Planned future default.

items: Choose a mode with `--proxy-mode` or the `mode` field in the kube-proxy config file. Windows only has `kernelspace`.
Service ClusterIPs come from the `--service-cluster-ip-range` set on kube-apiserver.
That flag seeds a default **ServiceCIDR** object named `kubernetes`. List ranges with `kubectl get servicecidrs`, and allocated IPs with `kubectl get ipaddresses`.

flashcards.front: What IP does a Pod get?
flashcards.back: Its own IP address, unique across the whole cluster.

flashcards.front: How do two containers in the same Pod talk to each other?
flashcards.back: Over localhost. They share the Pod's network namespace.

flashcards.front: Is NAT used for Pod-to-Pod traffic across nodes?
flashcards.back: No. Pods reach each other directly, without proxies or address translation.

flashcards.front: The four networking problems Kubernetes addresses?
Which components assign IPs to Pods, Services and Nodes?
flashcards.back: Pods: network plugin. Services: kube-apiserver. Nodes: kubelet or cloud-controller-manager.

flashcards.front: What is a CNI plugin for?
flashcards.back: It implements the Pod network (the Kubernetes network model). One is required.

flashcards.front: Default directories for CNI config and CNI binaries?
Since v1.24, who loads CNI plugins: the kubelet or the container runtime?
flashcards.back: The container runtime. The kubelet's cni-bin-dir and network-plugin flags were removed.
Service and EndpointSlice objects. It programs node rules so traffic to a ClusterIP reaches a backend.

flashcards.front: kube-proxy's default mode on Linux in v1.37?
flashcards.back: iptables (nftables is planned as a future default; ipvs is deprecated).

flashcards.front: Which kube-apiserver flag sets the range for Service ClusterIPs?
What happens to NetworkPolicy objects if the network plugin doesn't support them?
flashcards.back: The API still exists, but the policies have no effect.

questions.stem: A Pod has an app container and a sidecar. How can the sidecar reach the app's port 8080?

options.explanation: Containers in a Pod share one network namespace, so they talk over localhost.
A Service isn't needed inside a Pod; localhost works.

options.text: Through the node's IP and a hostPort
options.explanation: Host port mapping is not needed in the Kubernetes model.

options.text: They can't communicate over the network
options.explanation: They share the Pod's network namespace.

questions.stem: In the Kubernetes network model, traffic between Pods on different nodes must pass through NAT.

options.explanation: Pods talk to each other directly, without proxies or NAT.
Correct. Any Pod reaches any other Pod directly, on any node.

questions.stem: Which statements match the Kubernetes network model? Select 3.

options.text: Each Pod has a cluster-wide unique IP
options.explanation: Part of the model.

options.text: Node agents such as the kubelet can reach all Pods on their node
options.explanation: Part of the model.

options.text: Pods on different nodes can talk directly
options.explanation: The Pod network connects Pods on any node.

options.text: Every container gets its own Pod-level IP
options.explanation: The IP belongs to the Pod; its containers share it.

questions.stem: Which component is responsible for assigning IP addresses to Services?

options.explanation: The API server is configured with the Service IP range.
The network plugin assigns Pod IPs.
The kubelet (or cloud-controller-manager) assigns Node IPs.
kube-proxy routes Service traffic; it doesn't allocate Service IPs.

questions.stem: The Pod, Service and Node IP ranges in a cluster may overlap.

options.explanation: The ranges must be non-overlapping.
Correct. Kubernetes needs non-overlapping ranges for Pods, Services and Nodes.

questions.stem: In a dual-stack cluster, what must the network plugin, kube-apiserver and kubelet agree on?

options.explanation: All components must agree on which family is primary.

options.text: Using one shared CIDR for Pods and Services
options.explanation: Ranges must not overlap.
Dual-stack means both IPv4 and IPv6 are assigned.

questions.stem: On Linux, what usually implements the Pod network itself?

options.explanation: Most runtimes use CNI to talk to the Pod network implementation.
kube-proxy handles Service proxying, not the Pod network.
CoreDNS provides name resolution, not Pod connectivity.
The scheduler places Pods on nodes.

questions.stem: New Pods on one node get no network. Where would you check, by default, that a CNI configuration file exists?

options.explanation: That is the default CNI configuration directory.
That holds static Pod manifests, not CNI config.
That's the default directory for CNI binaries, not config.
That flag was removed in v1.24.

questions.stem: Since Kubernetes v1.24, the container runtime, not the kubelet, is responsible for loading CNI plugins.

options.explanation: The kubelet's cni-bin-dir and network-plugin flags were removed in v1.24.
CNI management is no longer in scope for the kubelet.

questions.stem: Which CNI plugin provides hostPort support?

options.explanation: portmap, with the portMappings capability, supports hostPort.
bandwidth provides traffic shaping.
loopback provides the lo interface for each sandbox.

questions.stem: Which objects does kube-proxy watch to program Service routing? Select 2.

options.explanation: kube-proxy watches Services.
kube-proxy watches EndpointSlices to know the backends.
Ingress is handled by an Ingress controller.
NetworkPolicy is usually enforced by the network plugin.

questions.stem: kube-proxy runs with no mode set on a Linux v1.37 node. Which mode does it use?

options.explanation: iptables is the default in v1.37.
nftables is planned to become the default in a future release.
ipvs is deprecated since v1.35 and isn't the default.
kernelspace is the only mode on Windows.

questions.stem: Which Service type does kube-proxy NOT implement a virtual IP for?

options.explanation: kube-proxy handles every Service type other than ExternalName.
ClusterIP is the core virtual IP that kube-proxy implements.
kube-proxy handles NodePort traffic too.
